questions.q: In the 6th century BCE, a farmer lives beside the Indus River, and a scribe from Iran arrives with the army of the Persian emperor who has gained control of the region. (b) Which name for the region does the chapter link with each of them, 'Sindhu' or 'Hindu'?
questions.a: (a) The farmer, because inhabitants are people who live in a particular place; the Persian scribe is a visitor from outside. (b) The farmer goes with 'Sindhu', the earlier name of the Indus region; the Persian scribe goes with 'Hindu' (or 'Hind', 'Hidu'), the Persians' adaptation of 'Sindhu' in their language.
s: (a) The farmer, since inhabitants are people who live in a place and the scribe comes from outside

questions.q: Manoj says: 'All the old names of India reach us from ancient texts written in India, so a historian of names needs no other kind of source.' Is Manoj right? Give your verdict and two examples from the chapter to support it.
questions.a: No, Manoj is wrong. The chapter says India's names come to us from ancient texts, accounts of travellers and pilgrims, and inscriptions. For example, Ashoka used the name 'Jambudvipa' in one of his inscriptions, and the Persians wrote 'Hind', 'Hidu' or 'Hindu' in their earliest records and stone inscriptions, which were not Indian texts at all.
s: Verdict: no, names also come from accounts of travellers and pilgrims, and from inscriptions
Example 1: Ashoka's inscription using 'Jambudvipa'
Example 2: Persian records and stone inscriptions using 'Hind', 'Hidu' or 'Hindu'

questions.q:
A history club in Bhopal is making a 50 cm paper strip that shows the last 5,000 years, at 1 cm for every 100 years. The right-hand end of the strip stands for today, and the club takes the present year as 2025. The club marks three points, at 500, 2,000 and 5,000 years ago, and adds a small picture of the carving on the north gate of the Great Sanchi Stupa, which shows a scene from rural India about 2,300 years ago.
(a) How far from the right-hand end should the Sanchi picture be placed?
(b) The club also puts a small sticker on the 500-years mark. How far apart, in cm, are this sticker and the Sanchi picture?
(c) A card for the ancient Tamil poem that praises a king, from about 2,000 years ago, goes on the 2,000-years mark. Is this card to the left or to the right of the Sanchi picture, and by how many cm?
(d) A picture of Emperor Ashoka's inscription, of about 250 BCE, is added last. About how far from the right-hand end should it go? Show your working.
questions.a: (a) 2,300 / 100 = 23 cm from the right-hand end. (b) The 500-years mark is 500 / 100 = 5 cm from the right-hand end, so the sticker and the picture are 23 - 5 = 18 cm apart. (c) The Tamil poem card is 2,000 / 100 = 20 cm from the right-hand end, so it is to the right of the Sanchi picture (nearer today), by 23 - 20 = 3 cm. (d) About 250 BCE is about 2,025 + 250 = 2,275 years before 2025, so the picture goes about 2,275 / 100 = 22.75 cm (about 23 cm) from the right-hand end, very close to the Sanchi picture.
s: (a) Finds 23 cm from the right-hand end
(b) Places the 500-years mark at 5 cm and finds the gap of 18 cm
(c) Places the Tamil poem at 20 cm: to the right of the Sanchi picture, by 3 cm
(d) Finds about 2,275 years ago and places Ashoka's inscription at about 22.75 cm (about 23 cm)

questions.q: Lalit says: 'Sapta Sindhava is a name that comes from the Rig Veda, and it covered the whole of India, from Kashmir down to Kerala.' Is Lalit fully right, partly right or wrong? Give your verdict and two reasons.

Regions like Kashmira and Kerala are names we meet later, in the Mahabharata.

Wrong part: it names only the northwest region, not the whole land from Kashmir to Kerala

questions.q: Compare the names 'Sapta Sindhava' and 'Bharatavarsha' under three heads: (a) the text each comes from, (b) the area each name covers, (c) what each name is built on.

(b) 'Sapta Sindhava' covers only the northwest region of the Subcontinent; 'Bharatavarsha' extends to the entire Subcontinent. (c) 'Sapta Sindhava' is built on rivers (the land of the seven rivers); 'Bharatavarsha' is built on a people (the country of the Bharatas, a main Vedic group).
s: (a) Rig Veda for Sapta Sindhava; Mahabharata for Bharatavarsha
(b) Northwest region only, against the entire Subcontinent
(c) Built on rivers, against built on a people (the Bharatas)

questions.q:
The chapter says that 'Sindhu' refers to the Indus River, or at times to a river in general. Kavitha writes four sentences for a class quiz. For each sentence, write which sense of 'Sindhu' it uses, 'the Indus River' or 'a river in general', and give a one-line reason.
(a) 'The land of Sapta Sindhava had seven sindhus.'
(b) 'In the 6th century BCE a Persian emperor gained control of the region of the Sindhu.'
(c) 'Every sindhu in the hills carries water down to the plains.'
(d) 'The Greek name Indoi came, through Persian, from the Sindhu.'
questions.a: (a) A river in general: seven different rivers cannot all be the Indus. (b) The Indus River: the chapter says the Persian emperor gained control of the region of the Indus River, which was earlier called 'Sindhu'. (c) A river in general: the sentence speaks of every river in the hills, not of one particular river. (d) The Indus River: the chapter's summary says foreign names such as 'Indoi' were derived from the Sindhu or Indus River.
s: (a) A river in general, since seven rivers cannot all be the Indus
(b) The Indus River, the region the Persian emperor took
(c) A river in general, since it means every river in the hills
(d) The Indus River, from which the foreign names were derived

questions.q:
A Class 6 group in Amritsar is building a table model titled 'Sapta Sindhava'. Each river is to be shown by a strip of blue ribbon 15 cm long, and they have one large board cut in the shape of the whole Subcontinent. Their draft label reads: 'Sapta Sindhava: a name for the whole of India, taken from the Mahabharata.' The exhibition opens tomorrow, and there is time to make only ONE fix: either cut the board down to the region the name really covers, or rewrite the label.
(a) Going by the meaning of the name, how many strips does the model need, and how many centimetres of ribbon in all?
(b) Point out the two errors in the draft label.
(c) The longest strip is to carry the word 'Sindhu'. Which river does 'Sindhu' usually refer to?
(d) Which ONE fix should the group make? Justify, and say what your choice still leaves wrong.
questions.a: (a) 7 strips, since the name means 'the land of the seven rivers'; 7 x 15 = 105 cm of ribbon. (b) The name is from the Rig Veda, not the Mahabharata; and it names the northwest region of the Subcontinent, not the whole of India. (c) The Indus River. (d) Rewrite the label, for example 'Sapta Sindhava: the Rig Veda's name for the northwest region of the Subcontinent'. This corrects both errors in the label (the text and the area it claims), while cutting the board would correct only the area and leave the wrong text on display. What it still leaves wrong: the board keeps the shape of the whole Subcontinent, so the model's shape does not match the new label.
s: (a) 7 strips and 105 cm of ribbon
(b) Names both errors: Rig Veda not Mahabharata, and the northwest region not the whole of India
(c) The Indus River
(d) Chooses to rewrite the label because it corrects both written errors, and notes that the board's whole-Subcontinent shape is still left unmatched

questions.q:
A Class 6 group in Pune is making a floor puzzle of the land with six tiles, one for each region that the chapter's text names from the Mahabharata: Kashmira, Kurukshetra, Vanga, Pragjyotisha, Kaccha and Kerala. Their teacher's note gives where the modern places lie: Kashmir and Haryana in the north, Bengal and Assam in the east, Kutch in the west, Kerala in the south. There is time to paint only four tiles, and the rule is that the painted tiles must include at least one region from each of north, east, west and south.
(a) Which two tiles must be painted in every set that follows the rule? Explain using their modern places.
(b) How many different sets of four tiles follow the rule? Show how you worked it out.
(c) Ravi wants to paint Kashmira, Kurukshetra, Vanga and Kerala. Does his set follow the rule? If not, which direction is missing?
(d) The teacher now allows only three tiles, which must include Kaccha and Kerala. Can three tiles still show all four directions? Which tiles could be the third one?
questions.a: (a) Kaccha and Kerala. Kaccha is today's Kutch, the only region in the west, and Kerala is the only region in the south, so without them the west or the south would be missing. (b) The other two tiles must be one from the north (Kashmira, more or less today's Kashmir, or Kurukshetra, parts of Haryana) and one from the east (Vanga, parts of Bengal, or Pragjyotisha, roughly Assam). That gives 2 x 2 = 4 sets. (c) No. Kashmira and Kurukshetra are north, Vanga is east and Kerala is south; Kaccha is left out, so the west is missing. (d) No: three tiles can cover at most three directions. With Kaccha (west) and Kerala (south), the third tile can be any one of Kashmira or Kurukshetra (north) or Vanga or Pragjyotisha (east), and either the east or the north is then left out.
s: (a) Kaccha and Kerala, the only regions in the west and the south
(b) One north tile (2 choices) and one east tile (2 choices): 2 x 2 = 4 sets
(c) No: Kaccha is left out, so the west is missing
(d) No, three tiles cover at most three directions; the third tile is any one of Kashmira, Kurukshetra, Vanga or Pragjyotisha, leaving out east or north

questions.q:
A children's encyclopedia has this entry:
'JAMBUDVIPA: an island in the Indian Ocean, named after the mango tree. The name is found only in Ashoka's inscriptions. Ashoka used it in about 250 CE for the land that is India today, and no more.'
Find the errors in this entry. For each one, write what the chapter actually says, and then write a corrected entry of two or three sentences.
questions.a: Errors: (1) It is not an island in the ocean; 'Jambudvipa' came to mean the Indian Subcontinent. (2) It is named after the jamun tree (also called the jambul or Malabar plum tree), not the mango. (3) The name is not only in Ashoka's inscriptions; the Mahabharata also uses it. (4) Ashoka's date is about 250 BCE, not CE. (5) His Jambudvipa was the whole of India at that time, which included what is today Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan, not only today's India. Corrected entry: 'Jambudvipa, the island of the fruit of the jamun tree, is a name the Mahabharata uses for the Indian Subcontinent. In about 250 BCE, Emperor Ashoka used it in an inscription for the whole of India, which then included today's Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan.'
s: Corrects 'island in the ocean': the name came to mean the Indian Subcontinent
Corrects the tree: the jamun (jambul, Malabar plum) tree, not the mango
Corrects 'only in Ashoka's inscriptions': the Mahabharata also uses it
Corrects 250 CE to about 250 BCE and the area to include today's Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan
Writes a correct two- or three-sentence entry

Joseph draws a plain outline of the Subcontinent and writes four labels around it: 'snowy mountains' along the top, 'ocean' along the bottom, 'Cape Kumari' at the southern tip, and 'oceans' on the left and the right sides. He took the labels from two ancient sources in the chapter.

(c) The Himalayas. (d) The Vishnu Purana, which says the country between those limits 'is called Bharata'. The Tamil poem praises a king whose name is known across those limits, so it gives the land's limits but no name for the land.

(b) About 2,000 years old
(c) The Himalayas
(d) The Vishnu Purana, because it names the land Bharata; the Tamil poem praises a king and gives no name for the land

questions.q:
Two schools, one in Jaipur and one in Kochi, meet in a radio quiz called 'Our Land in Old Words'. A correct answer scores 2 points and a wrong answer loses 1 point. Both teams start at 0.
Round 1: Jaipur is read the line 'The country that lies north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains is called Bharata' and is asked its source; it answers 'the Vishnu Purana'. Kochi is asked how old the chapter's ancient Tamil poem praising a king is; it answers 'about 200 years'.
Round 2: Jaipur is asked in which year the Constitution of India came into force; it answers '1947'. Kochi is asked: 'Bharata became the name generally used for the Subcontinent a few centuries after the time of which emperor?'; it answers 'Ashoka'.
(a) Mark each Round 1 answer right or wrong, giving the correct answer where needed.
(b) Mark each Round 2 answer right or wrong, giving the correct answer where needed.
(c) Work out each team's final score. Is there a winner?
(d) Kochi's captain appeals: 'Our Round 1 answer should be accepted, and then we win by 3 points.' Check both parts of her appeal.
questions.a: (a) Jaipur is right: the line is from the Vishnu Purana. Kochi is wrong: the poem is about 2,000 years old, not 200. (b) Jaipur is wrong: the Constitution came into force in 1950. Kochi is right: the chapter says 'Bharata' became the general name a few centuries after Ashoka's time (about 250 BCE). (c) Jaipur: 2 - 1 = 1 point. Kochi: -1 + 2 = 1 point. It is a tie, 1 point each, so there is no winner. (d) Her arithmetic is right: if the Round 1 answer were accepted, Kochi would have 2 + 2 = 4 points against Jaipur's 1, a lead of 3. But the answer cannot be accepted, because the poem is about 2,000 years old, so the appeal fails and the result stays a tie.
s: (a) Jaipur right (Vishnu Purana); Kochi wrong, the poem is about 2,000 years old
(b) Jaipur wrong, the Constitution came into force in 1950; Kochi right (Ashoka)
(c) Jaipur 1 point, Kochi 1 point: a tie, no winner
(d) The arithmetic (4 against 1, a lead of 3) is right, but the answer stays wrong (about 2,000 years), so the appeal fails

questions.a: (a) In the Rig Veda, where it refers to one of the main Vedic groups of people; so the word is indeed older than Ashoka. (b) 'The country of the Bharatas'. (c) 'Jambudvipa'. (d) The chapter says that 'a few centuries later', after Ashoka's time, 'Bharata' became the name generally used for the Indian Subcontinent, and it quotes the Vishnu Purana. (e) Her two facts are true, but her conclusion is wrong. An old word is not the same as the usual name for the land: Ashoka himself used 'Jambudvipa' for the whole of India, and 'Bharata' became the general name only a few centuries later.
s: (a) The Rig Veda, where Bharata is one of the main Vedic groups of people
(b) The country of the Bharatas
(c) Jambudvipa
(d) A few centuries after Ashoka's time; the Vishnu Purana
(e) Concludes the claim is wrong: her facts are true, but Ashoka used Jambudvipa and Bharata became the general name only later

questions.q:
A class in Bhubaneswar plays a relay game called 'Pass the Name'. Four players stand in a line. Player 1 is a person living by the Indus long ago, Player 2 is an ancient Persian scribe, Player 3 is an ancient Greek writer and Player 4 is a modern English speaker. Each player must pass the name on, changing it only in the way the chapter says that people changed it. Player 1 starts by saying 'Sindhu'. Then a fifth student, playing an ancient Chinese scholar, asks to join the line.
(a) What can Player 2 say?
(b) What change does Player 3 make, and why?
(c) What name does Player 4 end with?
(d) Should the Chinese player take her name from Player 2 or from Player 3? Justify using the Chinese chain of names.
questions.a: (a) 'Hind', 'Hidu' or 'Hindu'. (b) Player 3 drops the first letter 'h', giving 'Indoi' or 'Indike', because the letter 'h' did not exist in the Greek language. (c) 'India'. (d) From Player 2. The chapter gives the Chinese chain as Sindhu, Hindhu, Indu, Yindu: it passes through the Persian-style form 'Hindhu' and then 'Indu', and never through the Greek 'Indoi' or 'Indike', so the Chinese name branches off after the Persian step.
s: (a) Hind, Hidu or Hindu
(b) Drops the 'h' to make Indoi or Indike, because Greek had no 'h'
(c) India
(d) Chooses Player 2, using the chain Sindhu, Hindhu, Indu, Yindu, which does not pass through the Greek form

questions.q: Put these four events in the order in which they happened, from earliest to latest, taking the present year as 2025: (i) the first use of 'Hindustan' in a Persian inscription, about 1,800 years ago; (ii) Xuanzang's journey from China to India, in the 7th century CE; (iii) a Persian emperor gaining control of the Indus region, in the 6th century BCE; (iv) Ashoka's inscription using 'Jambudvipa', about 250 BCE. Show your working, and find roughly how many years passed between Ashoka's inscription and the first use of 'Hindustan'.
questions.a: 1,800 years before 2025 is about 225 CE. The 6th century BCE (600 to 501 BCE) comes before 250 BCE, because larger BCE numbers are earlier. So the order is: (iii) the Persian campaign, (iv) Ashoka's inscription, (i) the first use of 'Hindustan' (about 225 CE), (ii) Xuanzang's journey (601 to 700 CE). From about 250 BCE to about 225 CE is roughly 250 + 225 = 475 years, nearly five centuries.
s: Converts 'about 1,800 years ago' into about 225 CE
Places the 6th century BCE before 250 BCE (larger BCE numbers are earlier)
Gives the full order: Persian campaign, Ashoka, Hindustan, Xuanzang
Finds the gap of roughly 475 years between Ashoka and the first use of Hindustan

questions.a: (a) The Hindi version says 'Bharat arthath India', putting Bharat first, so the order of the two names changes with the language and tells us nothing about which name is older. (b) The Rig Veda, India's most ancient text, several thousand years old, where 'Bharata' refers to one of the main Vedic groups of people. (c) In the 6th century BCE a Persian emperor took the Indus region, earlier called 'Sindhu', and the Persians' records called the land 'Hind', 'Hidu' or 'Hindu'; based on these Persian sources the Greeks, who had no 'h', made it 'Indoi' or 'Indike', and this led eventually to 'India'. (d) The word Bharata appears in the Rig Veda, which is several thousand years old; the Persian name Hindu appears only from the 6th century BCE, so the word Bharata appears first. (A student who notes that the root 'Sindhu' is itself in the Rig Veda, as in 'Sapta Sindhava', and so says the two roots cannot be ranked this way, should also get this mark.) (e) Rukmini's argument is wrong: the order of the names in a phrase depends on the language, as the Hindi version shows, so it cannot prove that India is the older name.
s: (a) Hindi version 'Bharat arthath India' puts Bharat first, so word order changes with the language
(b) The Rig Veda, where Bharata is one of the main Vedic groups
(c) India traced from Sindhu through Persian Hind, Hidu or Hindu (6th century BCE) and Greek Indoi or Indike
(d) Compares: the word Bharata in the Rig Veda (several thousand years old) comes before the Persian Hindu (6th century BCE); also accept that the root Sindhu is itself in the Rig Veda
(e) Concludes the argument is wrong because word order depends on the language and does not show age
